decisionMemo.businessProblem: A mid-tier department store chain is declining: revenue fell from $850M (FY2023) to $800M (FY2025) and EBITDA margin compressed from 6% to 4%. Same-store sales decline ~4% per year while inventory accumulates (+~12%) and markdowns deepen, indicating the company is buying and operating its 45-store footprint to a demand forecast that the market no longer delivers. Fixed real-estate and store-labor costs do not flex down, so margin de-leverages as revenue shrinks. The central question: is the deterioration a structural mismatch between the company's demand/footprint plan and actual sustainable demand (over-forecasted store base and inventory), a competitive displacement problem, or a pure cost-structure problem? Without store-level demand and contribution analysis, the chain risks either closing the wrong stores or continuing to overbuy inventory against an outdated forecast.

rootCauseDiagnosis.description: Supply-demand imbalance due to forecast error or inventory misalignment
rootCauseDiagnosis.mechanismDescription: Demand signal not correctly translated to supply plan. Excess inventory ties up cash; stockouts lose revenue. Forecast error causes bullwhip effect through supply chain.
alternativeExplanations: Demand may be genuinely volatile (external shock)
Supply chain constraint may be the binding constraint

scenarios.name: Aggressive Recovery (Best Case)
scenarios.description: Execute all interventions in optimal sequence with full team commitment
assumptions: Team capacity fully available (no other initiatives)
Client budget approved for all recommended interventions
No external market shocks during implementation
scenarios.expectedOutcome: Revenue recovery within 90 days, competitive positioning restored
risks: Cascading failures if one intervention stumbles

Team capacity for 1-2 major initiatives at a time
